## Prepare DESeq2, limma or edgeR results for lisaR {#preparing-de-inputs--introduction}


Start with the complete result table from a differential-expression model that
you have already fitted. This guide shows two routes:

- use your exported table directly and name its columns in the lisaR study
  file; or
- use `prepare_lisa_de_input()` to create standard column names and a
  row-level audit.

The adapter is optional. It does not fit a model, choose a comparison or prove
which software produced a table.

The worked tables below are small fictional examples. The gene names make the
code easy to follow, but the numbers are not measurements. Use your complete
tested table for a real study.

<span id="choose-the-direct-or-adapted-route"></span>

### Choose the direct or adapted route {#preparing-de-inputs--choose-the-direct-or-adapted-route}

Your input needs one row per gene and these five values:

| Value | What to supply |
|---|---|
| Gene identifier | A non-empty identifier that matches the TERM2GENE membership resource. |
| Effect | The model's effect for the chosen comparison, such as `log2FoldChange` or `logFC`. |
| Signed ranking statistic | A statistic for the same comparison, ordered towards the declared positive direction. |
| P-value | The unadjusted p-value from the fitted model. |
| Adjusted p-value | The model's adjusted p-value for the complete tested population. |

If the exported table already contains these values, save it as TSV and point
`symbol_col`, `logfc_col`, `rank_col`, `pvalue_col` and `padj_col` to
the existing names in the study file. A DESeq2 Wald `stat` or a limma
moderated `t` can be used directly. You do not need to create
`rank_value`.

Use the adapter when standard names or its audit will make the hand-off
clearer. It returns `symbol`, `log2FoldChange`, `rank_value`, `pvalue`
and `padj`, ready to be named in a study file. The adapter works on an
exported data frame without loading DESeq2, limma or edgeR.

<span id="state-the-comparison-and-positive-direction"></span>

### State the comparison and positive direction {#preparing-de-inputs--state-the-comparison-and-positive-direction}

Before saving either form, write down the model comparison and what a positive
effect means. The signed statistic must describe the same comparison. Keep the
producing software, model specification and original export with the prepared
file.

| Input | Suitable starting point | What not to infer |
|---|---|---|
| DESeq2 Wald result | Signed `stat` for the stated coefficient/contrast | A DESeq2 likelihood-ratio `stat` need not be signed |
| limma one-contrast result | Signed moderated `t` | A multi-coefficient F statistic does not have one direction |
| edgeR one-contrast result | An explicitly declared signed ranking derived for that contrast | The adapter cannot infer direction from unsigned F/LR |
| Any result | Complete tested table, with original adjusted p-values | A significant-only table is not the GSEA universe |

Use the complete tested table rather than filtering to `padj < 0.05` before
GSEA. Non-significant genes remain part of the ordered background against
which a set is evaluated. Retain the adjusted p-values calculated for the
original tested population.

<span id="adapt-a-deseq2-style-wald-table"></span>

### Adapt a DESeq2-style Wald table {#preparing-de-inputs--adapt-a-deseq2-style-wald-table}

This fictional result has six tested genes. One has no statistic and another
has a finite ranking but no adjusted p-value, illustrating why absence of an
adjusted p-value should not silently remove a row from the saved table.

```{r deseq2-table, eval=TRUE}
library(lisaR)

wald <- data.frame(
  gene = c("CXCL9", "GZMB", "MKI67", "TCF7", "IL7R", "CCR7"),
  log2FoldChange = c(1.4, 0.8, -0.7, 0.15, -0.2, NA_real_),
  stat = c(4.2, 2.1, -2.8, 0.4, -0.6, NA_real_),
  pvalue = c(0.00003, 0.036, 0.005, 0.69, 0.55, NA_real_)
)
wald$padj <- p.adjust(wald$pvalue, method = "BH")
wald$padj[5L] <- NA_real_  # Illustrative missing adjusted p-value.

prepared <- prepare_lisa_de_input(
  wald,
  method = "DESeq2",
  columns = list(symbol = "gene"),
  positive_direction = "treated relative to control",
  matrix_scale = "transformed"
)
prepared$data

stopifnot(
  nrow(prepared$data) == nrow(wald),
  identical(prepared$data$rank_value, wald$stat),
  is.na(prepared$data$padj[5L]),
  prepared$row_audit$rank_eligible[5L],
  !prepared$row_audit$rank_eligible[6L]
)
```

The output columns are `symbol`, `log2FoldChange`, `rank_value`, `pvalue` and
`padj`. No threshold has been applied. The missing statistic remains missing;
it is not replaced by zero. `rank_eligible` records a finite ranking value,
not biological validity or every downstream eligibility condition.

Inspect what the adapter actually declared:

```{r input-audit, eval=TRUE}
prepared$column_mapping
prepared$row_audit[c(
  "source_row", "source_id", "retained", "rank_eligible",
  "missing_rank", "missing_padj"
)]
prepared$receipt[c(
  "declared_method", "positive_direction", "rank_source",
  "significance_filter", "producing_software_verified"
)]
```

`producing_software_verified` is false because a data frame cannot establish
which software fitted its model. Retain the original table and model records;
the adapter's receipt is an input declaration, not independent provenance.

For real DESeq2 results, export the complete result for the intended contrast,
then convert it as above. Do not combine a statistic for one coefficient with
an effect from another. For likelihood-ratio results, choose and justify a
compatible signed statistic separately rather than relabelling an unsigned
statistic.

<span id="adapt-a-limma-result-with-its-moderated-t-statistic"></span>

### Adapt a limma result with its moderated t statistic {#preparing-de-inputs--adapt-a-limma-result-with-its-moderated-t-statistic}

For one specified limma coefficient or contrast, the conventional effect and
p-value columns are recognised. The gene column is still declared explicitly:

```{r limma-table, eval=TRUE}
limma_table <- data.frame(
  gene = c("CXCL9", "GZMB", "MKI67", "TCF7"),
  logFC = c(1.3, 0.7, -0.6, 0.1),
  t = c(4.8, 2.5, -3.2, 0.3),
  P.Value = c(0.0001, 0.018, 0.004, 0.77)
)
limma_table$adj.P.Val <- p.adjust(limma_table$P.Value, "BH")
limma_input <- prepare_lisa_de_input(
  limma_table, method = "limma",
  columns = list(symbol = "gene"),
  positive_direction = "treated relative to control"
)
stopifnot(
  identical(limma_input$data$rank_value, limma_table$t),
  nrow(limma_input$data) == nrow(limma_table)
)
limma_input$data
```

When exporting a real `topTable()`, request all tested rows rather than its
default small top table, and use the intended single contrast. If biological
identifiers are in non-default row names, declare
`columns = list(symbol = ".rownames")`. Default row numbers are not gene IDs.

<span id="declare-a-signed-edger-ranking"></span>

### Declare a signed edgeR ranking {#preparing-de-inputs--declare-a-signed-edger-ranking}

An edgeR F or likelihood-ratio statistic is unsigned. For a **single
one-degree-of-freedom contrast**, one possible ranking convention is
`sign(logFC) * sqrt(F)`, using the effect for that same contrast. This is a
declared ranking transformation, not a new p-value or a claim that it is a
limma moderated t statistic. The design and test metadata must establish the
one-contrast restriction; the numbers in an exported table cannot prove it.

The following fictional example explicitly assumes that restriction:

```{r edger-table, eval=TRUE}
edger_table <- data.frame(
  symbol = c("CXCL9", "GZMB", "MKI67", "TCF7"),
  logFC = c(1.2, 0.6, -0.5, 0.1),
  F = c(16, 6.25, 9, 0.09),
  PValue = c(0.0008, 0.02, 0.006, 0.77)
)
edger_table$FDR <- p.adjust(edger_table$PValue, "BH")
edger_table$signed_sqrt_F <-
  sign(edger_table$logFC) * sqrt(edger_table[["F"]])

edger_input <- prepare_lisa_de_input(
  edger_table, method = "edgeR",
  columns = list(rank = "signed_sqrt_F"),
  positive_direction = "treated relative to control"
)
stopifnot(
  identical(edger_input$data$rank_value, edger_table$signed_sqrt_F),
  identical(edger_input$data$padj, edger_table$FDR)
)
edger_input$data
```

For a multi-degree-of-freedom F or LR test, **do not attach the sign of an
arbitrarily chosen logFC**. Return to the fitted model and define a meaningful
one-dimensional contrast, or choose a method appropriate to the original
multidimensional question. Renaming `F` to `signed_rank` does not make it signed.

The adapter requires the rank mapping for edgeR and rejects conventional
unsigned F/LR columns and p-value/FDR columns as rankings. It also checks sign
agreement where both the rank and effect are finite and nonzero. Those checks
detect some mistakes; they cannot establish that a declared transformation was
scientifically justified.

<span id="resolve-orientation-missing-values-and-duplicates"></span>

### Resolve orientation, missing values and duplicates {#preparing-de-inputs--resolve-orientation-missing-values-and-duplicates}

<span id="orientation"></span>

#### Orientation {#preparing-de-inputs--orientation}

`positive_direction` describes the effect in words. With the default
`rank_direction = "same_as_effect"`, the ranking must follow it too. If the
ranking really encodes the reverse comparison while the effect is correct,
`rank_direction = "opposite_to_effect"` negates the rank once and records the
choice. It does not reverse the effect, rename a contrast or repair mixed
model coefficients.

<span id="missing-values"></span>

#### Missing values {#preparing-de-inputs--missing-values}

The default `na_policy = "retain"` saves missing statistics and records their
status. `na_policy = "error"` instead rejects them. Missing/empty identifiers,
infinite values and malformed numbers always fail. Keep model-specific reasons
such as filtering, non-convergence or independent filtering beside the source
table; the adapter does not reconstruct them.

<span id="duplicate-identifiers"></span>

#### Duplicate identifiers {#preparing-de-inputs--duplicate-identifiers}

The default is an error, including case-insensitive collisions. Investigate
whether two rows are transcripts, aliases, repeated exports or distinct
features mapped to the same gene. Do not average their logFC, statistics or
p-values.

An explicit row-selection policy is available when it is justified. This toy
example demonstrates its audit, not a recommended biological rule:

```{r duplicate-audit, eval=TRUE}
duplicated_source <- rbind(wald, wald[1L, , drop = FALSE])
selected <- prepare_lisa_de_input(
  duplicated_source, "DESeq2",
  columns = list(symbol = "gene"),
  positive_direction = "treated relative to control",
  duplicate_policy = list(
    type = "select", criterion = "max_abs_rank", tie_breaker = "row_number"
  )
)
stopifnot(
  nrow(selected$full_data) == 7L,
  nrow(selected$data) == 6L,
  sum(!selected$row_audit$retained) == 1L
)
selected$row_audit[c("source_row", "source_id", "retained")]
```

The repeated row is preserved in `full_data` and its disposition is recorded.
On real non-identical duplicates, selecting the largest absolute statistic
can favour stronger effects. Choose the policy before interpretation and
retain the mapping/selection evidence. See the input contract in
[Configuration reference](configuration-resources-and-execution.html#configuration-reference--introduction) for row-level mapping
policies.

<span id="expression-matrices-are-a-separate-input"></span>

### Expression matrices are a separate input {#preparing-de-inputs--expression-matrices-are-a-separate-input}

The adapter only records `matrix_scale`; it neither reads nor transforms a
matrix, and that argument is not a YAML configuration field. Use
`matrix_scale = "transformed"` in the adapter receipt for values already
transformed, such as VST, rlog or documented log2 expression. Record
`"count_like"` only for count-like values. This declaration does not itself
configure downstream heatmaps. Their matrix-path convention is separate; see
the configuration reference before attaching a matrix. Do not describe VST
values as raw counts or apply a second log transform by accident.

Match matrix feature IDs to DE IDs, review sample order/annotation, and keep the
transformation and filtering provenance. An effect/ranking table cannot
reconstruct sample-level expression. The standard gene-evidence view can show
DE values without an expression matrix; expression heatmaps need that separate
input.

<span id="save-the-adapted-table-and-its-audit"></span>

### Save the adapted table and its audit {#preparing-de-inputs--save-the-adapted-table-and-its-audit}

Write the prepared table and its audit into a new directory:

```{r save-prepared, eval=TRUE}
input_dir <- tempfile("prepared-de-inputs-")
stopifnot(!file.exists(input_dir))
dir.create(input_dir)

for (part in c(
  "data", "full_data", "receipt", "column_mapping",
  "row_audit", "duplicate_resolution"
)) {
  write.table(
    prepared[[part]], file.path(input_dir, paste0(part, ".tsv")),
    sep = "\t", quote = FALSE, row.names = FALSE, na = "NA"
  )
}
```

Retain the original source table and model record too: extra columns such as
model diagnostics are not copied into the canonical data.

The new folder contains the canonical TSV used by lisaR and the audit files
that explain how it was made. Keep the original export and model record beside
this folder.

Point the analysis configuration at `data.tsv` with this column mapping. This
is a fragment to place in the complete study file created in the next guide:

```yaml
single_de:
  - analysis_id: treated_vs_control
    label: Treated versus control
    comparison: Treated minus control
    positive_direction: Higher in treated than control
    de_path: prepared-de-inputs/data.tsv
    species: Homo sapiens
    symbol_col: symbol
    logfc_col: log2FoldChange
    rank_col: rank_value
    pvalue_col: pvalue
    padj_col: padj
```

For the adapted route, the rank column is now `rank_value`, not the original
`stat` or `t`. For the direct route, keep the original column name in
`rank_col`. Relative paths are interpreted from the folder containing the
configuration file.

The six-row example is too small for a real enrichment analysis. Apply the
chosen route to your complete tested results, then follow
[Getting started](preparing-and-analysing-your-data.html#getting-started--introduction) to validate resources, plan,
run and verify the study.

For supported DESeq2/edgeR objects already in memory, the alternative local API
is documented in [Function reference](functions-and-workflows.html#function-reference--introduction). It is
separate from this table-first workflow; no object file needs to be
deserialised to follow this page.

## Use your own differential-expression table {#use-your-own-de--introduction}


Once [Riaz ON](worked-examples.html#riaz-on-quick-start--introduction) runs, replace its table with your own.
Supply the complete DE result, not only significant genes.

<span id="prepare-the-input"></span>

### Prepare the input {#use-your-own-de--prepare-the-input}

For a DESeq2 table, use these columns:

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `symbol` | Gene symbol matching the gene-set resource. |
| `log2FoldChange` | Signed effect for your comparison. |
| `stat` | Signed ranking statistic, normally the Wald statistic. |
| `pvalue` | Gene-level raw P value. |
| `padj` | Gene-level adjusted P value. |

Check which group is in the numerator before writing the direction sentence.
A DESeq2 likelihood-ratio statistic is unsigned; the
[extended R guide](preparing-and-analysing-your-data.html#getting-started--introduction) explains that case and edgeR/limma
inputs.

### Run one analysis {#use-your-own-de--run-one-analysis}

This example assumes a human DESeq2 Wald-test result and the resource prepared
during Riaz ON. If you skipped that optional example, first prepare the
corresponding membership resource with
[`prepare_lisa_msigdb_resource()`](functions-and-workflows.html#function-reference--prepare_lisa_msigdb_resource)
after reviewing its resource terms; see `?prepare_lisa_msigdb_resource`.
Resource acquisition is a separate manual step, not part of the offline
synthetic example. Change the two paths and the direction sentence.

```{r own-de, eval=FALSE}
library(lisaR)

result <- run_lisa(
  de = "de_treated_vs_control.tsv",
  output_dir = "lisa-treated-vs-control",
  species = "Homo sapiens",
  method = "DESeq2",
  positive_direction = "Higher in treated than in control"
)

stopifnot(identical(result$gate, "PASS"))
check <- verify_lisa_run(result$output_dir)
stopifnot(identical(check$gate, "PASS"))
browseURL(result$report_index)
```

Choose a new output directory. STANDARD is the default; it includes PNG and
SVG figures, source tables and figure recipes. Add `pdf = TRUE` if needed.

lisaR uses the supplied DE results. It does not re-estimate your effects or fit
your experimental design. For another species, prepare the corresponding
[membership resource](configuration-resources-and-execution.html#resources-and-provenance--introduction); do not substitute the
human resource.

**Next: [Read your report](start-with-lisar.html#read-your-report--introduction).**

## Run lisaR with your prepared files {#getting-started--introduction}


For the short first-run route, use [Get started](start-with-lisar.html#quick-start--introduction). This
guide keeps the extended R examples and configuration options.

Use this guide to run lisaR on your differential-expression results and open
the HTML report. You do not need to write a configuration file or choose the
LISA dictionaries. The default output includes PNG and SVG figures, tables
and R scripts for reproducing the figures.

Install lisaR first, then follow the steps below. If you already use a YAML or
JSON study file, you can continue to pass it to `run_lisa()`.

If you want to practise without study data, use the self-contained
[Quick Start](start-with-lisar.html#quick-start--introduction). Its files and resources are synthetic and must
not be reused as the gene universe for a real study.

<span id="what-you-need"></span>

### What you need {#getting-started--what-you-need}

- a complete differential-expression table, not only the significant rows;
- one sentence stating what a positive effect means in your comparison; and
- gene-set memberships for your species, prepared in the first step below.

[Prepare differential-expression inputs](preparing-and-analysing-your-data.html#preparing-de-inputs--introduction) explains the
table conventions. DESeq2 tables use the usual column names by default.
For edgeR or limma tables, specify `method = "edgeR"` or `method = "limma"`.
The ranking statistic must have a sign; the optional input examples below
show how to declare it.

<span id="prepare-the-gene-set-membership-resource-once"></span>

### 1. Prepare the gene-set membership resource, once {#getting-started--prepare-the-gene-set-membership-resource-once}

lisaR ships its LISA dictionaries and category hierarchy. They assign gene sets
to biological categories, but they do not contain the genes in each set. That
membership comes from MSigDB and is prepared once per machine.

Read the [MSigDB terms](https://www.gsea-msigdb.org/gsea/msigdb_license_terms.jsp)
before running this command. Set `accept_terms = TRUE` only if you accept them.

```{r prepare-membership, eval=FALSE}
library(lisaR)

msigdb <- prepare_lisa_msigdb_resource(accept_terms = TRUE)
```

If you already hold an authorised MSigDB ZIP, use the local-file form described
in [Resources and provenance](configuration-resources-and-execution.html#resources-and-provenance--introduction). Do not point a
real study at the sample project's 40-gene TERM2GENE resource.

After registration, `run_lisa()` selects the resources for the species you
specify. If a required resource is missing, it tells you what to prepare
before starting the analysis.

### 2. Run one analysis {#getting-started--run-one-analysis}

This is a complete first run. Replace the path, the species and the direction
sentence with your own.

```{r run-one, eval=FALSE}
result <- run_lisa(
  de                 = "de_treated_vs_control.tsv",
  output_dir         = "lisa-treated-vs-control",
  species            = "Homo sapiens",
  positive_direction = "higher in treated than in control"
)

```

`de` also accepts the data frame itself or a DESeq2 Wald-test
`DESeqResults` object. With an explicit `positive_direction`, native DESeq2
results refuse missing or empty mapped symbols; resolve the ID mapping rather
than silently dropping tested rows. For DESeq2 likelihood-ratio tests and edgeR results,
see the input examples below. `positive_direction` has no default: lisaR never infers which
side of a comparison a positive effect belongs to.

Choose a new folder for `output_dir`; lisaR will create it. If an input or
argument is rejected before the analysis starts, correct it and repeat the
call with the same folder name.

By default this produces a standard report with PNG and SVG figures, the source
data tables and the figure reproduction recipes. PDF is off unless you ask for
it.

The configured `run_lisa()` workflow calculates category inference after the
gene-set analyses. For each semantic collection, the default category view
shows adjusted-P stars (up to `****` at P ≤0.0001); the card retains the exact
P and minimum supported count d/N. This is separate from the descriptive
mean NES and from a comparison between two completed analyses.

Check that the analysis completed successfully:

```{r verify-one, eval=TRUE}
# The evaluated verifier uses the accepted distributed synthetic run.
# For your own analysis, keep result$output_dir from the preceding manual call:
# check <- verify_lisa_run(result$output_dir)
# Extract the shipped complete saved run to a new temporary directory.
fixture_dir <- tempfile("lisa-saved-fixture-")
dir.create(fixture_dir)
utils::untar(system.file("extdata", "p5-tiny-scientific-run.tar.gz",
  package = "lisaR", mustWork = TRUE), exdir = fixture_dir)
saved_run <- file.path(fixture_dir, "p5-tiny-scientific-run", "run")
check <- verify_lisa_run(saved_run)
stopifnot(identical(check$gate, "PASS"))
check[c("gate", "artifact_type")]
```

These checks should both return `"PASS"`. Verification checks the saved
files without repeating the analysis. You can then open the report:

```{r open-one, eval=FALSE}
browseURL(file.path(result$output_dir, "report_index.html"))
```

`result$reports` lists the available report pages. Keep the whole output
folder together when moving or sharing it so that the links continue to work.

If either gate is not `"PASS"`, keep the message and the output folder, and
follow [Troubleshooting](reports-and-exploration.html#troubleshooting--introduction).

<span id="compare-two-analyses"></span>

### 3. Compare two analyses {#getting-started--compare-two-analyses}

A contrast compares two completed LISA profiles. Declare the orientation
explicitly: `contrast = c("ON", "PRE")` means **ON minus PRE**. The order of
`de` never decides it.

```{r run-two, eval=FALSE}
result <- run_lisa(
  de = list(
    PRE = "de_pre_vs_control.tsv",
    ON  = "de_on_vs_control.tsv"
  ),
  output_dir = "lisa-pre-on",
  species    = "Homo sapiens",
  positive_direction = list(
    PRE = "higher at baseline than in its control",
    ON  = "higher on therapy than in its control"
  ),
  contrast = c("ON", "PRE"),
  title    = "Baseline versus on-therapy"
)

result$reports[result$reports$page == "contrasts", ]
```

The contrast page states the declared orientation. A positive value means a
larger mean NES in `ON` than in `PRE`. That mean is descriptive: it is not a
category-level significance test, and it is not another
differential-expression test.

For more than one contrast, supply a list of pairs. Each pair specifies its
own order.

<span id="optional-settings"></span>

### Optional settings {#getting-started--optional-settings}

The steps above are enough to run an analysis and read its report. The
sections below cover output options and less common input formats.

<span id="adjust-what-is-produced"></span>

#### Adjust what is produced {#getting-started--adjust-what-is-produced}

The first example needs no output settings. Add options only when you want
to change what lisaR produces:

```{r adjust, eval=FALSE}
result <- run_lisa(
  de                 = "de_treated_vs_control.tsv",
  output_dir         = "lisa-study",
  species            = "Homo sapiens",
  positive_direction = "higher in treated than in control",
  svg                = FALSE,       # PNG only
  recipes            = FALSE,       # no figure recipes
  collections        = c("GOBP-C2", "GOMF"),
  workers            = 4L
)
```

Use `dry_run = TRUE` to inspect a plan without calculating enrichment or
building the report.

For a new analysis, `mode = "full"` writes one report in the same
`output_dir`: the standard report plus every applicable FULL figure (member
gene sets, prioritized genes, volcano overlays, gene heatmaps, recurrent
genes, contrast profiles and paired products), each placed in its analysis,
collection and category. FULL can take substantially longer and use several
gigabytes. To add figures to an existing STANDARD result without repeating
enrichment, use `plan_lisa_extension()` followed by `render_lisa_categories()`,
which writes its own gallery, as shown in
[The HTML report](reports-and-exploration.html#scientific-report--introduction).

For settings without a dedicated argument, use `pipeline` or `report`.
Unspecified settings keep their defaults:

```{r advanced-overrides, eval=FALSE}
result <- run_lisa(
  de                 = "de_treated_vs_control.tsv",
  output_dir         = "lisa-study",
  species            = "Homo sapiens",
  positive_direction = "higher in treated than in control",
  report             = list(evidence_max_sets = 40L),
  pipeline           = list(run_hallmarks = TRUE)
)
```

Specify each setting in one place: as a direct argument, or inside `pipeline`
or `report`. Repeating a setting is rejected, even when both values agree.

<span id="tables-that-need-an-explicit-column-mapping"></span>

#### Tables that need an explicit column mapping {#getting-started--tables-that-need-an-explicit-column-mapping}

lisaR reads the usual DESeq2, edgeR and limma column names. Name the columns
when yours differ, or when the statistic to rank on is not the conventional
one:

```{r columns, eval=FALSE}
result <- run_lisa(
  de                 = "limma_treated_vs_control.tsv",
  output_dir         = "lisa-limma-study",
  species            = "Homo sapiens",
  positive_direction = "higher in treated than in control",
  method             = "limma",
  columns            = list(symbol = "gene", rank = "t")
)
```

Some ranking statistics have no sign and need an explicit choice:

- a DESeq2 likelihood-ratio result, whose `stat` is unsigned;
- an edgeR result, whose `F` and `LR` statistics are unsigned.

For an edgeR **one-dimensional comparison**, choose the signed effect size
as the ranking if that matches your analysis. This complete synthetic example
fits a model and explicitly selects one treated-versus-control coefficient:

```{r edger, eval=TRUE}
set.seed(1729)
group <- factor(rep(c("control", "treated"), each = 3),
                levels = c("control", "treated"))
baseline <- seq(40, 240, length.out = 60)
effects <- rep(c(2, 0.5, 1), length.out = length(baseline))
means <- vapply(group, function(g)
  baseline * if (g == "treated") effects else 1, numeric(length(baseline)))
counts <- matrix(stats::rnbinom(length(means), mu = as.vector(means), size = 8),
  nrow = length(baseline),
  dimnames = list(paste0("GENE", seq_along(baseline)),
                  paste0("sample", seq_along(group))))
dge <- edgeR::calcNormFactors(edgeR::DGEList(counts = counts, group = group))
design <- stats::model.matrix(~ group)
# A fixed dispersion is declared for this synthetic illustration only.
fit <- edgeR::glmFit(dge, design = design, dispersion = 0.1)
x <- edgeR::glmLRT(fit, coef = "grouptreated") # exactly one df: treated-control
tt <- edgeR::topTags(x, n = Inf, sort.by = "none", adjust.method = "BH")
original <- tt$table
# Choose signed logFC itself as an effect-size ranking. This is not sign(LR),
# nor a signed multi-df F statistic. Positive values mean higher in treated.
tt$table$signed_rank <- tt$table$logFC
prepared <- prepare_lisa_de_input(tt,
  columns = list(rank = "signed_rank"),
  positive_direction = "higher in treated than control")
stopifnot(identical(tt$table[, names(original), drop = FALSE], original),
  identical(rownames(prepared$full_data), rownames(original)),
  identical(prepared$full_data$pvalue, original$PValue),
  identical(prepared$full_data$padj, original$FDR),
  nrow(prepared$full_data) == nrow(original))

```

The preparation above is self-contained. After preparing the scientific
membership resource for your study, the following analysis remains a manual
template; it is not executed during the offline documentation build.

```{r edger-analysis, eval=FALSE}
result <- run_lisa(
  de                 = tt,
  output_dir         = "lisa-edger-study",
  species            = "Homo sapiens",
  positive_direction = "higher in treated than control",
  columns            = list(rank = "signed_rank")
)
```

The signed ranking is your modelling decision; lisaR records it and does not
derive one for you. Here it is logFC for the declared one-df contrast, not a
signed F/LR statistic for a joint test.

`topTags()` performs the FDR adjustment chosen in edgeR (BH in this example);
`n = Inf, sort.by = "none"` passes every tested row in source order.
`DGEExact` and `DGELRT` are rejected directly in all three DE entry points,
even if their table has user-added FDR/rank columns. Supply the prepared
`TopTags` object with your explicit signed ranking and declared direction.
lisaR does not choose or recalculate its P/FDR values or drop permitted NAs.

For a DESeq2 likelihood-ratio result, do not use its unsigned `stat` as the
ranking. Add a separately computed signed statistic for the comparison you
intend to interpret, then select it with `columns = list(rank = "signed_stat")`.

<span id="keep-your-results"></span>

### Keep your results {#getting-started--keep-your-results}

Keep the complete study folder, including `inputs/`, `results/` and
`study.json`. The JSON file records the settings used and can be passed back
to `run_lisa()` with its full path.

Keep the whole folder together with your original export and its model record.
lisaR does not fit or refit the differential-expression model.

If a run fails after creating `study.json`, keep the error message and folder.
Consult [Troubleshooting](reports-and-exploration.html#troubleshooting--introduction) before retrying the saved
configuration.

<span id="use-a-configuration-file"></span>

#### Use a configuration file {#getting-started--use-a-configuration-file}

Use a study file when you want to save and edit the complete configuration.
You can start from the `study.json` created by `run_lisa()`; the
[configuration reference](configuration-resources-and-execution.html#configuration-reference--introduction) explains its fields.

```{r config-route, eval=TRUE}
sample_project <- lisa_init_project(tempfile("lisa-input-config-"))
sample_config <- file.path(sample_project, "study.yml")
validation <- validate_lisa_config(sample_config, check_files = TRUE)
validation$readiness
stopifnot(validation$execution_ready)
plan <- plan_lisa_outputs(sample_config)
plan$summary
# To execute your own reviewed configuration manually:
# result <- run_lisa("study.yml")
```

Existing configuration files keep their previous defaults. To include SVG and
recipes, use this structure:

```yaml
report:
  formats:
    svg: true
  recipes: true
```

When passing a configuration file, edit settings in that file rather than
adding the direct-input arguments to the same call.

<span id="continue-with-a-prepared-scientific-example"></span>

### Continue with a prepared scientific example {#getting-started--continue-with-a-prepared-scientific-example}

The [Riaz RNA-seq example](worked-examples.html#riaz-gse91061-worked-example--introduction) and
[CPTAC proteomics example](worked-examples.html#cptac-ccrcc-proteomics--introduction) provide prepared DE
tables, source context and complete study configurations. Follow the instructions for the chosen example. Its gene-set memberships
belong to that example and should not be used for unrelated studies.

The evaluated examples use the R session recorded here. Manual network,
archive and GUI templates are not claimed as executed by this record.
